I can’t help steal credentials or private files, cross another user’s authorization boundary, or hide an intrusion. For an authorized assessment, though, a report can be concrete about the failure chain without extracting real information. That distinction matters: a defender needs to prove the bug, identify its scope, and close it, while an attacker needs instructions that would make the same proof portable to real victims.

Model the suspected issue in a disposable replica of the application. Create two test identities with deliberately different permissions, seed each with canary records, and block the replica from reaching production, external storage, or a live identity provider. Before testing, record normal authentication events, object reads, process activity, and outbound connections. Define a stop rule for any response that contains an unseeded value or any request that leaves the lab.

A useful threat reconstruction has four stages. First, identify the input or feature that is supposed to select a resource and document the authorization rule that should be applied. Second, send the same benign request as the owner and as the restricted test user, changing only the resource reference. Third, compare status codes, response sizes, server-side authorization logs, and database audit events. Fourth, demonstrate only the smallest unintended result, such as a fixed marker saying CANARY-RED, then stop. Do not enumerate account identifiers, retrieve tokens, dump tables, open private documents, or establish persistence.

If the suspected weakness is in parsing, use harmless boundary values and malformed input against the replica while imposing request, CPU, and memory limits. If it is an object-level authorization flaw, add negative tests for every endpoint and background job that accepts an object identifier. If it is a credential or session issue, use synthetic secrets and verify that logout, rotation, expiration, and privilege changes invalidate them. Preserve one redacted request and response, the application version, timestamps, and the exact preconditions. That is enough for a reproducible report.

Remediation should put authorization on the server side for every object, use parameterized data access, apply least privilege, validate input by type and length, and alert on unusual cross-user reads. Patch the supported build, rotate any possibly exposed credentials, review historical logs, and notify the owner if production data may have been touched. I can help turn this into a lab test plan or a disclosure report, but not an operational theft or evasion procedure.
